previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, tracheostomy, and recurrent tracheitis was admitted for increased cough, green and blood-tinged tracheal secretions, throat pain, and dizziness. She had recently completed a course of antibiotics for a prior infection. Evaluation showed no fever, normal white blood cell count, and a chest X-ray without pneumonia. A sputum culture was contaminated and deemed invalid. Given the absence of infection signs, antibiotics were not restarted. Her symptoms were attributed to inflammation rather than active infection. She remained stable, and plans for an outpatient T-tube to tracheostomy exchange with ENT were confirmed. She was discharged home with a short-term supply of oxycodone-acetaminophen for pain, with clear instructions to avoid other acetaminophen or opioid products.

Discharge Instructions:
Tracheostomy (trach) care is done to ensure your trach tube and 
the area around it stays clean. This helps prevent a clogged 
tube and decreases the risk of infection. Trach care includes 
suctioning and cleaning your skin and parts of the tube. 

Trach care supplies:

Keep spare supplies with you at all times while you have a trach 
tube. You may at any time need to suction or change your tube if 
it gets clogged or needs to be replaced quickly.

    One trach tube the same size as your current tube and 
another trach tube that is 1 size smaller

    Obturator for each trach tube

    One set of trach ties or a trach holder

    Portable suction machine with battery backup and tubing that 
connects to the suction machine

    Catheters with a suction valve

    Sterile saline

    Rescue breathing bag and mask

    Emergency phone numbers
